sections.title: Ordered Field Axioms
sections.focus: Axioms for addition, multiplication, and order; cancellation; inverses; signs and inequalities.
sections.homework: The Chapter 1 exercise set revisits which axioms fail in N and Z, midpoint and AM-GM inequalities, and proofs from the axioms.

sections.title: Absolute Values
sections.focus: Absolute value as distance, basic inequalities, the triangle inequality, reverse triangle inequality, and the epsilon test for equality.
sections.homework: Chapter 1 exercises use absolute value in max/min formulas, bounds, and comparison arguments.

sections.title: The Completeness Axiom
sections.focus: Maximum and minimum, upper and lower bounds, bounded sets, supremum and infimum, and completeness.
sections.homework: Chapter 1 exercises ask for bounds, suprema and infima and prove how these behave under subsets, sums, products, and scalar multiplication.

sections.title: Density of Q and R - Q
sections.focus: Unboundedness of N, the Archimedean property, density of rationals and irrationals, and the irrationality of sqrt(2).
sections.homework: Chapter 1 exercises revisit density proofs, the omitted sign cases, square-root existence, and rational multiples of sqrt(2).

sections.title: Chapter 1 Exercises
sections.focus: A cumulative review of ordered-field arguments, inequalities, bounds, completeness, density, and proof techniques.
sections.homework: This section is the Chapter 1 homework set itself; its quizzes emphasize choosing proof steps, counterexamples, and correct conclusions.

sections.title: Limits of Sequences
sections.focus: The epsilon-N definition, convergence and divergence, uniqueness of limits, and translating symbolic inequalities into an N choice.
sections.homework: Exercises use the definition for rational, exponential, alternating, and radical sequences and ask for examples and counterexamples.

sections.title: Algebraic Properties of Limits of Sequences
sections.focus: Limit laws, boundedness of convergent sequences, order and squeeze theorems, absolute values, products, quotients, and roots.
sections.homework: Exercises combine convergent and divergent sequences, compute limits, and prove omitted algebraic and order properties.

sections.title: Accumulation Points
sections.focus: Neighborhood definitions of accumulation point, isolated points, examples, and the relation between infinite bounded sets and accumulation points.
sections.homework: Exercises construct sets with prescribed accumulation points and prove interval and finiteness statements.

sections.title: Monotonic Sequences
sections.focus: Increasing and decreasing sequences, bounded monotone convergence, recursive sequences, and the first Bolzano-Weierstrass formulation.
sections.homework: Exercises classify sequences, find bounds, construct monotone approximations to suprema/infima, and analyze recursive sequences.

sections.title: Cauchy Sequences
sections.focus: The Cauchy definition, convergence implies Cauchy, boundedness, and completeness of R via the Cauchy criterion.
sections.homework: Exercises prove specific sequences are Cauchy and analyze a recursively defined averaging sequence.

sections.title: Subsequences
sections.focus: Subsequence indices, preservation of limits, dominant terms, monotone subsequences, Bolzano-Weierstrass, and subsequence criteria for convergence.
sections.homework: Exercises find subsequences and limits, relate accumulation points to subsequences, and use interlacing and convergence criteria.

sections.title: Limits of Functions
sections.focus: Epsilon-delta limits on arbitrary domains, accumulation points, uniqueness, one-sided behavior, and changing a function at the limit point.
sections.homework: Exercises prove limits from the definition, simplify removable discontinuities, and construct functions with or without limits.

sections.title: Limits of Sequences and Functions
sections.focus: The sequential criterion for function limits, algebraic limit laws, order theorem, and squeeze theorem.
sections.homework: Exercises use sequences to disprove limits, prove limit laws, and evaluate or establish function limits.

sections.title: The Definition of Continuity
sections.focus: Continuity at a point and on a domain, the role of isolated points, and Lipschitz-type estimates.
sections.homework: Exercises prove continuity directly, explore isolated points, and introduce the Lipschitz condition.

sections.title: Limits and Continuity
sections.focus: Sequential continuity, continuity as equality of value and limit, algebraic properties, composition, and continuity of standard functions.
sections.homework: Exercises prove consequences of continuity, max/min continuity, compositions, and local boundedness.

sections.title: Uniform Continuity
sections.focus: Uniform versus pointwise continuity, epsilon-delta quantifiers, Lipschitz functions, compact-interval uniform continuity, and sequential criteria.
sections.homework: Exercises prove uniform continuity or failure on specified intervals and connect Lipschitz estimates to uniform continuity.

sections.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
sections.focus: Bounded Value Theorem and Extreme Value Theorem for continuous functions on closed intervals.
sections.homework: There is no separate exercise list; practice emphasizes hypotheses, counterexamples when hypotheses are removed, and optimization existence.

sections.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
sections.focus: Bolzano's theorem, the Intermediate Value Theorem, fixed-point and root applications, images of intervals, and continuity of inverses.
sections.homework: Exercises bracket roots, prove fixed-point and crossing results, and use IVT to analyze polynomial and range questions.

sections.title: Tangent Lines
sections.focus: Secant slopes approaching a tangent slope and the geometric interpretation of the derivative.
sections.homework: The preliminary Exercises 4.0 reinforce difference quotients, slopes of linear functions, and monotonicity.

sections.title: Linear Approximations
sections.focus: The tangent line as the best local linear approximation and the role of the limiting difference quotient.
sections.homework: Practice connects local error, slope, and the formula for a tangent-line approximation.

sections.title: Instantaneous Velocity
sections.focus: Average velocity, instantaneous velocity, and the derivative as a limit of average rates of change.
sections.homework: Practice interprets position functions, units, secant rates, and limiting velocity.

sections.title: The Definition of the Derivative
sections.focus: Derivative at a point, differentiability, derivatives from first principles, and differentiability implying continuity.
sections.homework: Exercises compute derivatives by definition, test nondifferentiability, and analyze zero and prescribed derivative conditions.

sections.title: Properties of the Derivative
sections.focus: Linearity, product and quotient rules, chain rule, inverse-function derivative, and power rules.
sections.homework: Exercises prove rules, differentiate compositions, and find tangent lines to inverse functions.

sections.title: Extrema and the Mean Value Theorem
sections.focus: Local extrema, Fermat, Rolle, Mean Value, zero derivative, and constant-difference theorems.
sections.homework: Exercises use MVT to bound changes, prove uniqueness/counting results, and compare functions through derivatives.

sections.title: First Derivative Tests
sections.focus: Derivative sign and monotonicity, strict monotonicity, critical points, and first derivative tests for extrema.
sections.homework: Exercises prove omitted cases and use derivative comparisons to establish inequalities and local behavior.

sections.title: l'Hopital's Rule
sections.focus: Extended Mean Value Theorem and l'Hopital's rule for 0/0 limits under stated hypotheses.
sections.homework: Exercises prove simplified forms and evaluate indeterminate limits.

sections.title: Area
sections.focus: Rectangle approximations, partitions, sample points, widths, and Riemann-sum intuition for nonnegative area.
sections.homework: Exercises later in 5.6 ask students to mimic area computations for polynomial functions.

sections.title: Distance
sections.focus: Distance traveled as accumulated nonnegative velocity and its approximation by velocity-times-time rectangles.
sections.homework: Practice translates between position, velocity, units, and accumulated distance.

sections.title: Riemann Sums
sections.focus: Riemann sums, dependence on tags and partitions, and bounding sums by lower and upper sums.
sections.homework: Homework in 5.6 computes concrete upper/lower sum differences and compares Riemann sums.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorems and Why They are Obvious
sections.focus: The two Fundamental Theorems interpreted through position, velocity, distance, and accumulation.
sections.homework: Practice distinguishes the two theorems and identifies the hypotheses and conclusions later proved formally.

sections.title: Partitions and Sums
sections.focus: Partitions, mesh, upper and lower sums, telescoping, refinement, and order relations among sums.
sections.homework: Exercises 5.6 use regular partitions, compute U-L, and mimic examples with polynomial and Dirichlet-type functions.

sections.title: Integrals
sections.focus: Upper and lower integrals, integrability as equality, and direct calculations for constants and simple functions.
sections.homework: Exercises calculate areas through sums and construct a nonintegrable function whose absolute value is integrable.

sections.title: Conditions for Integrability
sections.focus: The epsilon-partition criterion and integrability of monotone, continuous, and piecewise functions.
sections.homework: Exercises prove integrability for examples and omitted cases, and explore consequences of equality or small integral values.

sections.title: Algebraic Properties of the Integral
sections.focus: Linearity, additivity, order, absolute-value inequality, and integrability under algebraic operations.
sections.homework: Exercises prove negative scalar cases, products and max/min integrability, and zero-integral consequences.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
sections.focus: Oriented integrals, accumulation functions, both Fundamental Theorems, and differentiation/integration as inverse processes.
sections.homework: Exercises prove supporting results, study discontinuous examples, and apply FTC to inverse functions and integral-defined functions.

sections.title: Definitions and Basic Properties
sections.focus: Infinite series as limits of partial sums, geometric series, term test, p-series, and algebraic/order properties.
sections.homework: Exercises sum geometric series, test basic convergence, prove comparison properties, and manipulate convergent series.

sections.title: Tests for Convergence
sections.focus: Absolute and conditional convergence; direct and limit comparison, ratio, root, integral, and alternating-series tests; error bounds.
sections.homework: Exercises choose and justify convergence tests and prove consequences of absolute convergence and decreasing terms.

sections.title: Power Series
sections.focus: Power series, centers, convergence sets, radius and interval of convergence, and endpoint testing.
sections.homework: Exercises find intervals/radii and reason from coefficient limits and known convergence points.

sections.title: Properties of Power Series
sections.focus: Uniform convergence inside the radius, continuity, Abel-type endpoint behavior, and termwise integration and differentiation.
sections.homework: Exercises prove convergence properties and derive new power series by algebra, integration, and differentiation.

sections.title: Taylor Series
sections.focus: Taylor polynomials and series, Taylor coefficients, remainder estimates, and standard expansions.
sections.homework: Exercises build and modify Taylor series, approximate nonelementary integrals, and test whether functions equal a Taylor series.

questions.prompt: Let \(x\in\mathbb R\). Which statement correctly describes the additive inverse of \(x\)?
questions.explanation: An additive inverse of \(x\) is a real number whose sum with \(x\) is \(0\). Lemma 1.2.2 shows that this inverse is unique.

questions.prompt: Let \(x\in\mathbb R\) with \(x\ne0\). Which statement correctly describes the multiplicative inverse of \(x\)?
questions.explanation: A multiplicative inverse of a nonzero real number \(x\) is a real number \(y\) satisfying \(xy=1\). Lemma 1.2.2 shows that it is unique.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(x,y,z\in\mathbb R\). If \(x+z=y+z\), or if \(xz=yz\) with \(z\ne0\), which conclusion follows from Lemma 1.2.3 (Cancellation)?
choices: x and y have the same sign
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: \(x=y\).

questions.prompt: Suppose \(x,y\in\mathbb R\) and \(xy=0\). What conclusion follows from Lemma 1.2.6 (Divisors of Zero)?
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: x=0 or y=0.

questions.prompt: Which ordered-field axiom justifies adding the same number z to both sides of x<y?
questions.explanation: O3 states that order is preserved by addition of the same real number.

questions.prompt: If x<y and z<0, which inequality is correct?
questions.explanation: Multiplication by a negative reverses the inequality.

questions.prompt: Which step is the key to proving x*0=0 from the axioms?
questions.explanation: Distributivity creates two copies of x*0, and additive cancellation removes one.

questions.prompt: Which statement is always true when x ≠ 0?
questions.explanation: In an ordered field, a nonzero square is positive.

questions.prompt: In N={1,2,3,...}, which field axiom fails immediately?
questions.explanation: For example, 1 has no additive inverse inside N.

questions.prompt: In Z, which field axiom fails?
questions.correct: Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse in the set.
choices: Every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse in the set.
questions.explanation: For example, 2 has no reciprocal in Z.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(0<x<y\). Which reciprocal inequality follows from Lemma 1.2.8?
questions.explanation: Positive reciprocals reverse order: if \(0<x<y\), then \(0<y^{-1}<x^{-1}\).

questions.prompt: Which statement is exactly the trichotomy axiom O1 from the notes?
choices: For all \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), exactly one of \(x<y\), \(y<x\), or \(x=y\) holds.
For all \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), at least one of \(x\le y\) or \(y\le x\) holds, and both may fail.
questions.correct: For all \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), exactly one of \(x<y\), \(y<x\), or \(x=y\) holds.
questions.explanation: This is Axiom O1 as stated in Section 1.2.

questions.prompt: Which formula is the definition of \(|x|\) used in the notes?
questions.explanation: Definition 1.3.1 defines absolute value piecewise: use \(-x\) when \(x<0\) and \(x\) when \(x\ge0\).

questions.prompt: For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), which inequality is Theorem 1.3.3 (Triangle Inequality)?
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: \(|x+y|\le|x|+|y|\).

questions.prompt: For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), which inequality is Corollary 1.3.4?
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: \(\bigl||x|-|y|\bigr|\le|x-y|\).

questions.prompt: For r>0, which is equivalent to |x|<r?
questions.explanation: Absolute value bounds distance from zero in both directions.

questions.prompt: Which expression equals the distance between a and b?
questions.explanation: Distance on the real line is the absolute difference.

questions.prompt: Which formula is correct for \(\max(a,b)\)?
questions.explanation: If a≥b the formula reduces to a; if b≥a it reduces to b.

questions.prompt: Which formula is correct for \(\min(a,b)\)?
questions.explanation: Case analysis on a≥b or b≥a verifies the formula.

questions.prompt: To prove \(a=b\) using Theorem 1.3.5, which statement is sufficient to prove?
questions.explanation: The theorem says a real number is zero iff its absolute value is smaller than every positive ε.

questions.prompt: If |x-3|<2, what interval contains x?
questions.explanation: Rewrite as -2<x-3<2 and add 3.

questions.prompt: The shaded interval in the figure is centered at 2 and has radius 1. Which inequality describes it?
questions.explanation: Distance from \(x\) to 2 is \(|x-2|\); being inside the interval means that distance is less than 1.
questions.visual: Number line with the interval (1,3) highlighted conceptually

questions.prompt: Which statement is Theorem 1.3.5?
choices: \(x=0\) if and only if \(|x|<\varepsilon\) for every real \(\varepsilon>0\).
questions.correct: \(x=0\) if and only if \(|x|<\varepsilon\) for every real \(\varepsilon>0\).
questions.explanation: The theorem is used repeatedly later to prove equality by showing a difference is smaller than every positive real number.

questions.prompt: Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\). Which statement means that \(u\in\mathbb R\) is an upper bound of \(A\)?
choices: \(u\in A\) and \(a\le u\) for every \(a\in A\).
questions.explanation: Definition 1.4.9 says that \(u\) is an upper bound of \(A\) exactly when every element of \(A\) is at most \(u\). Membership \(u\in A\) is not required.

questions.prompt: Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) be bounded above. Which statement means that \(s=\sup A\)?
questions.correct: \(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\), and \(s\le u\) for every upper bound \(u\) of \(A\).
choices: \(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\), and \(s\le u\) for every upper bound \(u\) of \(A\).
\(s\in A\) and \(a\le s\) for every \(a\in A\).
\(s\) is a lower bound of \(A\), and every lower bound is at most \(s\).
questions.explanation: Definition 1.4.17 defines the supremum as the least upper bound. It need not be an element of \(A\).

questions.prompt: Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\). Which statement means that \(m=\max A\)?
questions.correct: \(m\in A\) and \(a\le m\) for every \(a\in A\).
choices: \(m\in A\) and \(a\le m\) for every \(a\in A\).
\(a\le m\) for every \(a\in A\), whether or not \(m\in A\).
\(m\) is the least upper bound of \(A\), whether or not it belongs to \(A\).
questions.explanation: Definition 1.4.1 requires a maximum to be an element of the set and to be at least as large as every element of the set.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) is nonempty and bounded above. What does Axiom 1.4.27 (Completeness Axiom) guarantee?
questions.correct: A has a supremum in R.
choices: A has a supremum in R.
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: A has a supremum in R.

questions.prompt: For A=(0,1), which statement is correct?
questions.correct: sup A=1, but A has no maximum.
choices: sup A=1, but A has no maximum.
questions.explanation: The number 1 is the least upper bound but does not belong to the open interval.

questions.prompt: For \(A=\{1/n:n\in\mathbb N\}\), which statement is correct?
questions.correct: inf A=0 and min A does not exist.
choices: inf A=0 and min A does not exist.
questions.explanation: All terms are positive and approach 0, but 0 is not a term.

questions.prompt: If A is a subset of B and both are nonempty and bounded, which chain is correct?
questions.correct: inf B ≤ inf A ≤ sup A ≤ sup B
choices: inf B ≤ inf A ≤ sup A ≤ sup B
inf A ≤ inf B ≤ sup B ≤ sup A
questions.explanation: A smaller set can have a larger infimum and a smaller supremum.

questions.prompt: If k<0 and A is bounded, which identity is correct?
questions.explanation: Multiplication by a negative reverses order, so the largest scaled value comes from the smallest original value.

questions.prompt: To prove s=sup A, which two facts must be shown?
questions.correct: s is an upper bound of A, and every upper bound u satisfies s≤u.
choices: s is an upper bound of A, and every upper bound u satisfies s≤u.
s is in A, and A is finite.
s is a lower bound and belongs to A.
Every element of A equals s.
questions.explanation: These are exactly the upper-bound and leastness clauses.

questions.prompt: What is \(\sup\{r\in\mathbb Q:r^2<4\}\)?
choices: The set has no supremum in R.
questions.explanation: Rational numbers with square less than 4 approach 2 from below, and 2 is the least real upper bound.

questions.prompt: For the set \(A=(0,1)\), which statement correctly distinguishes extrema from bounds?
choices: \(\inf A=0\) and \(\sup A=1\), but \(A\) has neither a minimum nor a maximum.
questions.correct: \(\inf A=0\) and \(\sup A=1\), but \(A\) has neither a minimum nor a maximum.
questions.explanation: The endpoints bound the open interval and are its infimum and supremum, but neither endpoint belongs to the set.
questions.visual: Open interval (0,1)

questions.prompt: Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) be nonempty and bounded above. Which pair of conditions characterizes \(s=\sup A\)?
choices: \(a\le s\) for every \(a\in A\), and if \(u\) is any upper bound of \(A\), then \(s\le u\).
\(s\in A\), and \(s\le a\) for every \(a\in A\).
\(s\) is an upper bound and \(s\in A\).
questions.correct: \(a\le s\) for every \(a\in A\), and if \(u\) is any upper bound of \(A\), then \(s\le u\).
questions.explanation: A supremum is precisely a least upper bound.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the Archimedean Property (Theorem 1.5.3) as stated in the notes?
questions.correct: If \(x,y>0\), then there is \(n\in\mathbb N\) such that \(nx>y\).
choices: If \(x,y>0\), then there is \(n\in\mathbb N\) such that \(nx>y\).
Every bounded set has a maximum.
There is a largest natural number.
questions.explanation: In the notes, archimedean property is characterized by the condition in the correct choice: For x,y>0, some n in N satisfies nx>y.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(x<y\) are real numbers. What does Theorem 1.5.5 (Density of \(\mathbb Q\)) guarantee?
questions.correct: There is a rational r with x<r<y.
choices: There is a rational r with x<r<y.
Every number between x and y is rational.
x and y must be rational.
There is an integer between x and y.
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: There is a rational r with x<r<y.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(x<y\) are real numbers. What does Theorem 1.5.7 (Density of the Irrationals) guarantee?
questions.correct: There is an irrational s with x<s<y.
choices: There is an irrational s with x<s<y.
There are no rationals between x and y.
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: There is an irrational s with x<s<y.

questions.prompt: Which statement is equivalent to N not being bounded above in R?
questions.correct: For every real M, some n in N satisfies n>M.
choices: For every real M, some n in N satisfies n>M.
There is a largest natural number.
questions.explanation: Unbounded above means no real number bounds all natural numbers.

questions.prompt: Which statement follows from the Archimedean Property for every real number \(x>0\)?
questions.correct: There is n in N with 1/n<x.
choices: There is n in N with 1/n<x.
There is n with n<x for every x.
questions.explanation: Apply the property with y=1 and rearrange.

questions.prompt: Which assumption begins the standard proof by contradiction that \(\sqrt2\) is irrational?
choices: m and n are both odd without justification.
questions.explanation: Squaring then forces both m and n to be even, contradicting lowest terms.

questions.prompt: Why does density imply every nonempty open interval contains infinitely many rationals?
questions.correct: After finding one rational, apply density again to a smaller subinterval repeatedly.
choices: After finding one rational, apply density again to a smaller subinterval repeatedly.
Because an interval has integer length.
Because completeness directly gives a maximum rational.
questions.explanation: Density can be iterated in disjoint or nested subintervals.

questions.prompt: Which number is certainly irrational when r is a nonzero rational?
questions.explanation: If r/\(\sqrt{2}\) were rational, then \(\sqrt{2}\) would be a quotient of nonzero rationals.

questions.prompt: In a density proof for x<y, why choose n with n(y-x)>1?
questions.correct: It makes the scaled interval (nx,ny) longer than 1, so an integer can be placed inside.
choices: It makes the scaled interval (nx,ny) longer than 1, so an integer can be placed inside.
It proves x and y are integers.
It supplies a maximum of Q.
questions.explanation: After finding an integer m between nx and ny, m/n lies between x and y.

questions.prompt: If \(x<y\), what do Theorems 1.5.5 and 1.5.7 together imply?
choices: There is both a rational and an irrational number strictly between \(x\) and \(y\).
Every number between \(x\) and \(y\) is rational.
Every interval has a least rational number.
Every interval has a greatest irrational number.
questions.correct: There is both a rational and an irrational number strictly between \(x\) and \(y\).
questions.explanation: The notes prove density of \(\mathbb Q\) and of \(\mathbb R-\mathbb Q\) separately.

questions.prompt: Which strategy proves x<(x+y)/2<y from x<y?
questions.correct: Add x to x<y and add y to x<y, then divide the resulting inequalities by 2.
choices: Add x to x<y and add y to x<y, then divide the resulting inequalities by 2.
Use completeness to choose a maximum.
Assume x and y are integers.
questions.explanation: The ordered-field axioms preserve inequalities under addition and multiplication by the positive number 1/2.

questions.prompt: For \(x,y\ge0\), which nonnegative square leads directly to \(\sqrt{xy}\le\frac{x+y}{2}\)?
questions.explanation: Expanding gives \(x-2\sqrt{xy}+y\ge0\), which rearranges to the desired inequality.

questions.prompt: If S is bounded and s=sup S, what approximation property holds?
questions.correct: For every ε>0, some a in S satisfies s-ε<a≤s.
choices: For every ε>0, some a in S satisfies s-ε<a≤s.
There is always a=s in S.
Every a in S satisfies a<s-ε.
questions.explanation: Otherwise s-ε would be a smaller upper bound.

questions.prompt: If a≤b+1/n for every n in N, what follows?
questions.explanation: If a>b, choose n so large that 1/n<a-b, a contradiction.

questions.prompt: If A and B are bounded, what is sup(A+B)?
questions.explanation: Sums are bounded above by the sum of suprema, and elements can approach each supremum independently.

questions.prompt: When k<0, what happens to infimum and supremum under kA?
questions.correct: They exchange roles: sup(kA)=k inf A and inf(kA)=k sup A.
choices: They exchange roles: sup(kA)=k inf A and inf(kA)=k sup A.
questions.explanation: Negative scaling reverses order.

questions.prompt: Which set is a natural starting point for a completeness proof that every positive real number has a positive square root?
questions.correct: \(S=\{t\in\mathbb R:t\ge0\text{ and }t^2\le x\}\), and then show \((\sup S)^2=x\).
choices: \(S=\{t\in\mathbb R:t\ge0\text{ and }t^2\le x\}\), and then show \((\sup S)^2=x\).
Take \(S=\mathbb Q\) and assume it has a maximum.
questions.explanation: Completeness supplies the candidate supremum; inequalities rule out its square being too small or too large.

questions.prompt: Which pair need not be equal?
choices: sup A and the least upper bound of A
inf A and the greatest lower bound of A
max A and sup A when max A exists
questions.explanation: A supremum need not belong to A, so a maximum can fail to exist.

questions.prompt: For A=(2,3), which are upper bounds?
questions.explanation: Every element of A is less than 3, so any number at least 3 is an upper bound.

questions.prompt: What is inf{1/n:n is prime}?
questions.explanation: Prime numbers are unbounded, so their reciprocals approach 0; all are positive.

questions.prompt: If sup A belongs to A, why is it max A?
questions.correct: A supremum is an upper bound, and membership makes it an element of A.
choices: A supremum is an upper bound, and membership makes it an element of A.
Every supremum is automatically in A.
Completeness says every set has a maximum.
questions.explanation: The definition of maximum is exactly an upper bound that lies in the set.

questions.prompt: Which hypothesis is needed for sup(AB)=sup A sup B in the Chapter 1 exercise?
questions.correct: All elements of A and B are nonnegative.
choices: All elements of A and B are nonnegative.
questions.explanation: Without nonnegativity, order behavior of products is more complicated.

questions.prompt: Suppose \(S\subseteq\mathbb R\) and \(s=\sup S\). Which statement is the approximation property asked for in Exercise 1.6.20?
choices: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(a\in S\) such that \(s-\varepsilon<a\le s\).
There is one \(a\in S\) with \(s-\varepsilon<a\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
questions.correct: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(a\in S\) such that \(s-\varepsilon<a\le s\).
questions.explanation: If no element of \(S\) lay above \(s-\varepsilon\), then \(s-\varepsilon\) would be an upper bound smaller than \(s=\sup S\), a contradiction.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the definition that the sequence \(\langle s_n\rangle\) converges to \(L\)?
questions.correct: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(N\in\mathbb R\) such that for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), if \(n>N\), then \(|s_n-L|<\varepsilon\).
choices: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(N\in\mathbb R\) such that for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), if \(n>N\), then \(|s_n-L|<\varepsilon\).
There is one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(|s_n-L|<\varepsilon\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
For every \(N\in\mathbb R\), there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(n>N\) implies \(|s_n-L|<\varepsilon\).
There is \(N\in\mathbb R\) such that \(s_n=L\) for every \(n>N\).
questions.explanation: Definition 2.1.1 requires one tail of the sequence to lie inside every prescribed \(\varepsilon\)-tube about \(L\).

questions.prompt: Suppose a sequence \(\langle s_n\rangle\) converges both to \(L\) and to \(M\). What conclusion follows from Theorem 2.1.6 (Uniqueness of Limits)?
choices: L and M are both zero
questions.explanation: Under the hypotheses stated in the question, the result concludes: L=M.

choices: Agreement of more derivatives at the center and, with a controlled remainder, the approximation near the center.
The polynomial must equal the function everywhere.
The radius of convergence automatically becomes infinite.
questions.correct: Agreement of more derivatives at the center and, with a controlled remainder, the approximation near the center.
questions.explanation: Taylor polynomials match successive derivatives at the center; Taylor’s Formula controls the remainder under its hypotheses.

questions.prompt: If \(P_n\) is the Taylor polynomial of degree \(n\) for \(f\) at \(0\), how is the remainder \(R_n\) defined?
questions.explanation: Definition 6.5.7 defines the remainder as the error left after subtracting the Taylor polynomial from the function: \(R_n(x)=f(x)-P_n(x)\).
